canonical_topic: Nuclear power plant operation and thermal efficiency
definition: Nuclear plants generate electricity the same way coal plants do — heating water into pressurized steam that spins a turbine — but produce that heat via nuclear fission instead of combustion.
core_idea: Because the turbine technology is shared with coal plants, nuclear plants follow the same thermal-efficiency rule: higher operating temperature and continuous (non-cycling) operation yield more electricity per unit of fuel, with efficiency ranging roughly 25% for a low-temperature plant up to 50-60% for a larger, hotter one.
key_points: Steam-turbine technology is identical between nuclear and coal plants.
Higher operating temperature raises the fraction of heat energy converted to electricity.
A low-temperature plant may convert only ~25% of heat to electricity; a larger, hotter plant can reach 50-60%.
Plants are most efficient running full-time without letting the water cool overnight.
The key difference from coal is the heat source: nuclear fission vs. combustion.
relationships: Shares turbine/steam technology with coal-fired generation
Efficiency behavior parallels coal plant economics
trading_implications: Nuclear plants economically favor running as baseload (continuous full-time operation) rather than cycling, which affects their bidding behavior and price responsiveness in power markets.
caveats: Nuclear and coal plants are often thought of as fundamentally different generation technologies, but the electricity-generating turbine stage is the same; only the heat source differs.
